---
title: "Real data application: human brain cortex (Visium)"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", dpi = 96, out.width = "85%", fig.align = "center",
                      dev = "svg", dev.args = list(bg = "white"))   # vector graphics (SVG)
res <- readRDS("dlpfc_results.rds")
library(SigDoTS)
library(ggplot2)
n_dom <- length(res$fit_all$domain_nodes)
tt <- summary(res$fit_all)$tests
eta_all <- res$fit_all$tests$eta
```

This tutorial runs SigDoTS on a public 10x Genomics Visium section of human dorsolateral
prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), sample 151673 of Maynard et al. (2021). The cortex is organised in
layers, and this dataset comes with every spot labelled by hand with its layer (L1 to L6 and
white matter), so the result of SigDoTS can be compared with an answer that is known
independently. The section has `r format(res$n_spots, big.mark = ",")` spots over tissue.

The two runs below took `r sprintf("%.0f and %.0f seconds", res$timings[["whole_section"]], res$timings[["layer3"]])`
on `r res$n_cores` cores (`r res$date`, SigDoTS `r res$versions[["SigDoTS"]]`, R `r sub("R version ([0-9.]+).*", "\\1", res$versions[["R"]])`, BANKSY `r res$versions[["Banksy"]]`).
To keep this page quick to build, the code is shown as it was run and the results are loaded
from a saved file; running the code yourself gives the same results (same data, arguments and
seed).

As in the SigDoTS paper, the candidate domains come from BANKSY, a domain-detection method that
uses each spot's neighbourhood as well as its own expression, so that its candidate domains are
spatially coherent. The package's built-in k-means does not use positions and, on real tissue, gives
interleaved candidate domains that no merging can turn into layers (`cluster_method = "banksy"` below; the
Banksy package needs R 4.4 or later).

## The data

The section is available as a `SpatialExperiment` object from the Bioconductor package
STexampleData; the object holds the counts, the spot positions and the layer labels.

```{r load, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("BiocManager")
# BiocManager::install(c("STexampleData", "scuttle", "scran", "Banksy", "SingleCellExperiment"))
library(SigDoTS)
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(STexampleData)
library(scuttle)
library(scran)

spe <- Visium_humanDLPFC()          # downloads once (about 100 MB), then cached
spe
#> class: SpatialExperiment
#> dim: 33538 4992
#> ...
table(colData(spe)$ground_truth, useNA = "ifany")
```

```{r layers-table, echo = FALSE}
table(layer = res$layer, useNA = "ifany")
```

```{r layers-map, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "The spots of section 151673 coloured by their manually annotated cortical layer"}
lay <- data.frame(x = res$coords[, 1], y = res$coords[, 2], layer = res$layer)
ggplot(lay, aes(x, y, colour = layer)) + geom_point(size = 0.7) + coord_equal() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300", "#4a3aa7"),
                      na.value = "grey80", name = "Manual layer") +
  theme_void() + ggtitle("Section 151673: manual layer annotation") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

## Preparing the data

Four lines: keep the spots over tissue, drop genes with almost no counts, log-normalise, and
choose the 2,000 most variable genes. Any other normalisation and gene selection works as well.

```{r prepare, eval = FALSE}
spe <- spe[, colData(spe)$in_tissue == 1]            # 3,639 spots over tissue
spe <- spe[Matrix::rowSums(counts(spe)) >= 10, ]      # genes with at least 10 counts in all
spe <- logNormCounts(spe)                             # adds the "logcounts" assay
hvg <- getTopHVGs(modelGeneVar(spe), n = 2000)        # the 2,000 most variable genes
```

With Bioconductor 3.23 (scuttle 1.22, scran 1.40), `logNormCounts()`, `modelGeneVar()` and
`getTopHVGs()` print warnings that they, or functions they use, are deprecated in favour of the
newer package scrapper. They still work: in R 4.6.1 with these versions, the two runs below
give the same domains.

The positions are pixel coordinates in the tissue image, where rows count downwards. Flipping
the row axis makes the plots below appear the same way up as the image; the test does not
care, because it uses only distances between spots.

```{r coords, eval = FALSE}
coords <- spatialCoords(spe)
coords_plot <- cbind(x = coords[, "pxl_col_in_fullres"], y = -coords[, "pxl_row_in_fullres"])
```

## The whole section

The layers are the domains one expects, so `K0`, the number of candidate domains, is set above
the seven labels. With `K0 = 10`, BANKSY divides the section into 10 candidate domains (and every
simulated dataset into as many candidate domains as the part of the tree being tested has), and SigDoTS
decides which of them to merge.

```{r run-all, eval = FALSE}
fit <- sigdots(spe, coords = coords_plot, K0 = 10, genes = hvg, cluster_method = "banksy", n_cores = 10)
fit
```

```{r print-all, echo = FALSE}
print(res$fit_all)
```

SigDoTS keeps all `r n_dom` candidate domains: every one of the `r nrow(tt)` splits is
significant, with the observed statistic below that of every simulated single-domain dataset.
The map of the domains next to the manual layers:

```{r map-all, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "The domains SigDoTS found in section 151673"}
plot(res$fit_all)
```

How the domains relate to the layers (spots per domain and layer):

```{r table-all, echo = FALSE}
table(domain = domains(res$fit_all)$domain, layer = res$layer, useNA = "ifany")
```

The adjusted Rand index between the domains and the manual layers is
`r sprintf("%.2f", res$ari_whole_section)` (1 would be a perfect match, 0 no better than
chance). Two things explain the distance from 1. BANKSY's ten candidate domains cut the seven layers
finely: Layer 1 into two bands (domains 1 and 2), Layers 2 and 3 into two (6 and 7), the white
matter into three (8, 9 and 10), and the candidate domains covering Layers 4 to 6 (3, 4 and 5) each
straddle two layers. SigDoTS can only merge the candidate domains, so a domain follows BANKSY's
boundaries, and two layers that one candidate domain straddles cannot be separated. And SigDoTS
kept the within-layer bands: at each of those splits the two sides differ in mean expression
more than spatially correlated noise within one domain produces. Whether an outer and an
inner band of Layer 1, or white matter next to the cortex and deep white matter, are
different domains is a question for the biologist; the test reports that their expression
differs. With fewer candidate domains (`K0 = 7`), they would follow the layers more coarsely.

The tests, from the top of the tree:

```{r tests-all, echo = FALSE}
tt
```

```{r tree-all, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "The split tree of the whole-section run"}
plot(res$fit_all, type = "tree")
```

The spatial correlation that SigDoTS estimated for the single-domain model at the first test
(`plot(fit, type = "correlogram")`): `eta` is the share of the noise variance that is
spatially correlated, `ell` how far that correlation reaches, in units of the distance
between neighbouring spots. Here `eta` is `r sprintf("%.2f", eta_all[1])` (between
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(eta_all))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(eta_all))` over the nine tests):
once the candidate domains' means are removed, the expression of neighbouring spots is only
weakly correlated, so the simulated single-domain data are close to independent noise around
a common mean.

```{r correlogram-all, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, fig.alt = "Observed and fitted within-group correlation by distance, first test"}
plot(res$fit_all, type = "correlogram")
```

## A layer of interest: Layer 3

SigDoTS can be run on any subset of spots, for example the spots of one layer. Layer 3 is
anatomically one unit; BANKSY divides it into three candidate domains, and SigDoTS tests
whether the data support splitting it:

```{r run-l3, eval = FALSE}
l3 <- which(colData(spe)$ground_truth == "Layer3")
fit_l3 <- sigdots(spe[, l3], coords = coords_plot[l3, ], K0 = 3, genes = hvg, cluster_method = "banksy", n_cores = 10)
fit_l3
```

```{r print-l3, echo = FALSE}
print(res$fit_l3)
```

The split of Layer 3 is not significant (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(res$fit_l3)$tests$p_value[1])`:
`r res$fit_l3$tests$clearer[1]` of the `r summary(res$fit_l3)$tests$null_used[1]` simulated single-domain
datasets split at least as clearly), so SigDoTS reports Layer 3 as one domain and does not test
the lower split. On the left, BANKSY's three candidate domains; on the right, the one domain
that SigDoTS reports:

```{r map-l3, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.6, out.width = "100%", fig.alt = "Layer 3: BANKSY's three candidate domains (left) and the one domain SigDoTS reports (right)"}
# Two panels side by side (grid only, no other package): the candidate domains and the domains.
p_cand <- plot(res$fit_l3, type = "candidates") +
  labs(title = sprintf("Candidate domains (%d)", length(res$fit_l3$candidate_names)), subtitle = NULL)
p_dom <- plot(res$fit_l3) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Final domains (%d)", length(res$fit_l3$domain_nodes)), subtitle = NULL)
grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 2)))
print(p_cand, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(p_dom, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))
```

## Two details in the output

`summary(fit)` for the whole section lists, after the tests, the parts of the tree whose spots
fell into separate pieces on the 6-nearest-neighbour graph: Layer 1 is cut by a fold of the
section into pieces of 242, 49 and 14 spots, and a few single spots at the boundaries between candidate
domains have all their neighbours in other candidate domains. SigDoTS joins such pieces by their closest spots before
building the tree, so that every simulated dataset has a connected tree; nothing else changes.

```{r summary-all, echo = FALSE}
summary(res$fit_all)
```

The number of simulated datasets differs between tests (`null_used`): a test deep in the tree
has a small level, and SigDoTS simulates as many datasets as that level needs, stopping as soon
as the decision is certain.

## Writing the result back

`add_domains()` puts the domain of every spot into the object, next to the other per-spot
information, for whatever you do next:

```{r write-back, eval = FALSE}
spe <- add_domains(spe, fit)
head(colData(spe)[, c("ground_truth", "sigdots_domain", "sigdots_candidate_domain")])
```
